title: Ten-year clinical outcomes after successful percutaneous coronary intervention compared with medical treatment in patients with chronic total occlusion and preserved left ventricular ejection fraction
content:
by Hye Yon Yu, Jihun Ahn, Seung-Woon Rha, Byoung Geol Choi, Se Yeon Choi, Jae Kyeong Byun, Youjin Lee, Abiseka Panji Baskoro, Aditya Reza Pratama, Melly Susanti, Manda Satria Chesario, Soohyung Park, Cheol Ung Choi

Background

The long-term clinical benefit of revascularization in patients with chronic total occlusion (CTO) and preserved left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF ≥50%) remains uncertain.

Purpose

This study aimed to investigate the clinical impact of CTO revascularization in patients with preserved LVEF compared with those receiving optimal medical treatment (OMT) up to 10 years.

Methods

A total of 939 patients with CTO and preserved LVEF were analyzed, including those treated with OMT (OMT group; n = 492) or successful percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI group; n = 447). The primary endpoint was cardiac death, and the secondary endpoint was major adverse cardiac events (MACE) during a 10-year follow-up period. To adjust for baseline differences, inverse probability of treatment weighting (IPTW) was applied, yielding weighted cohorts of 934 OMT and 920 PCI patients. Time-to-event outcomes were evaluated using Kaplan–Meier analysis and Cox proportional hazards models. A Fine–Gray model was additionally used to account for competing non-cardiac death.

Results

After IPTW adjustment, the weighted sample sizes were 934 in the OMT group and 920 in the PCI group. During a median follow-up of 5.2 years (interquartile range, 2.9–10.0 years), the incidence of cardiac death was significantly lower in the PCI group than in the OMT group (2.0% vs. 6.3%, p = 0.001), whereas MACE did not differ significantly. The incidence of myocardial infarction (MI) was also lower in the PCI group (3.5% vs. 7.0%, p = 0.021). The cause-specific association with cardiac death (HR, 0.30; 95% CI, 0.14–0.65; p = 0.001) was attenuated in the Fine–Gray competing-risk analysis (sHR, 0.31; 95% CI, 0.10–1.02; p = 0.054). All-cause mortality and Hard MACE did not differ significantly between groups.

Conclusions

In CTO patients with preserved LVEF, successful CTO PCI was associated with a lower incidence of cardiac death during long-term follow-up compared with OMT. These findings suggest that successful CTO revascularization may have a favourable prognostic association in patients with preserved LVEF. However, this association was attenuated after accounting for competing non-cardiac death, warranting cautious interpretation of the potential long-term prognostic association.
